title: The Secret Garden
author: Frances Hodgson Burnett
ru: Одинокая избалованная девочка находит в старом поместье запертый сад — и вместе с ним дружбу, здоровье и радость жизни.

chapters.title: Chapter 1. A Girl from India
chapters.text:
Mary Lennox was ten years old, and she was not a nice child. She had a thin face, yellow skin and an angry look. She lived in India with her father and mother, but they never had time for her. Her mother liked parties and beautiful dresses. Servants looked after Mary and always did everything she wanted. So Mary never learned to say "please" or "thank you".

One hot summer a terrible illness came to the town. Many people died, and Mary's mother and father died too. The servants ran away. For two days nobody remembered the little girl in the empty house. Then some English officers found her.

"Who are you?" one of them asked.

"I am Mary Lennox," she said crossly. "Why did nobody come?"

Mary had no family in India. But she had an uncle in England, Mr Archibald Craven. He lived in a very old house called Misselthwaite Manor, in Yorkshire. So they put Mary on a ship and sent her to England.

In London a woman named Mrs Medlock met her. She was the housekeeper at Misselthwaite. They travelled north by train for many hours. The sky was grey and it was raining.

"Your uncle is a sad man," Mrs Medlock told her. "His back is crooked, and he is going to be away most of the time. The house has a hundred rooms, but most of them are locked. You must not walk around it."

Mary said nothing. She did not care. Late at night they drove across a dark, wide, empty land. "That is the moor," said Mrs Medlock. At last Mary saw a light far away. It was the house.

chapters.title: Chapter 2. Martha and the Locked Garden
chapters.text:
In the morning a young servant came into Mary's room to make a fire. Her name was Martha. She had round red cheeks and a friendly smile, and she talked a lot.

"Are you going to dress me?" asked Mary.

Martha laughed. "Can't you dress yourself? You're big enough!"

Mary was very angry. In India servants always dressed her. But Martha only laughed again, and after some time Mary put on her own clothes. It was the first time in her life.

Martha told her about her family. They lived in a small cottage on the moor. There were twelve children, and they were often hungry, but they were happy. Martha's mother was a kind and clever woman. Her brother Dickon was twelve. "He goes out on the moor every day," said Martha. "The birds and the animals love him. They aren't afraid of him at all."

"Go outside and play," Martha said. "There are big gardens round the house. But one garden is locked. Nobody has been in it for ten years."

"Why?" asked Mary.

"It was Mrs Craven's garden. She loved it. One day she was sitting on an old branch of a tree, and it broke. She fell and she died. After that, Mr Craven locked the door and buried the key. He doesn't let anybody go in."

Mary went out. She walked along long paths between high walls. Everything was grey and cold. In one garden she met an old gardener, Ben Weatherstaff. He was not friendly, but he was not unkind. A little bird with a red breast sat on a tree near him.

"That's a robin," said Ben. "He lives in the garden over the wall. He hasn't got any friends, just like you."

chapters.title: Chapter 3. The Key
chapters.text:
Every day Mary went outside. The cold wind from the moor made her cheeks pink, and she was hungry at dinner for the first time in her life. She was becoming stronger, but she was still lonely. She often thought about the locked garden. Where was the door?

One night there was a storm. The wind was crying round the house. But then Mary heard a different sound. It was a child crying somewhere in the house.

"What is that?" she asked Martha the next morning.

Martha looked afraid. "It's only the wind," she said quickly.

"No, it isn't," said Mary. "I heard a child."

But Martha did not answer, and she left the room.

A few days later Mary was walking near the high wall. The robin flew down and started looking for worms in some earth that a dog had just dug. Mary looked down. In the earth was an old rusty ring with a key on it.

"Perhaps it's the key to the garden!" she thought. Her heart was beating fast. She put the key in her pocket.

The next day the robin was on top of the wall. He was singing to her. Suddenly the wind blew hard and moved some long green ivy on the wall. Under the ivy Mary saw a round metal handle. It was a door!

She put the key into the lock. It was hard to turn, but it turned. Mary looked around. Nobody was there. She slowly opened the door, went in and closed it behind her.

She was standing inside the secret garden.

chapters.title: Chapter 4. Inside the Garden
chapters.text:
It was the strangest and most beautiful place Mary had ever seen. High walls stood all around it. There were many old rose bushes, and their long grey branches climbed over the walls and the trees. The grass was brown and dry. Everything was quiet.

"Is everything dead?" Mary whispered. "I hope it isn't."

She walked slowly across the grass. Then she saw some little green points coming out of the dark earth. They were very small, but they were alive!

"The garden isn't dead," she said happily. "These plants are going to grow."

But the grass and the weeds were too thick around them. So Mary found a sharp stick and began to dig. She cleared the earth around the green points so they had space and air. She worked for hours. She forgot about lunch. When she went back to the house, her face was pink and her eyes were bright.

"I want a little piece of garden," she told Martha. "I want to plant some flowers."

"Dickon can help you," said Martha. "He knows everything about plants. And he can buy seeds and some garden tools for you in the village."

Mary had a little money from her uncle, so Martha wrote to Dickon.

A few days later, Mary was walking in the park when she heard a strange, soft music. A boy was sitting under a tree and playing a wooden pipe. He had a round red face and very blue eyes. A squirrel, a pheasant and two rabbits were sitting near him and listening.

"Don't move," he said quietly. "You'll frighten them. I'm Dickon. I know you're Miss Mary."

chapters.title: Chapter 5. Dickon
chapters.text:
Dickon had the seeds and the tools. He smiled at Mary, and it was a warm, open smile. Mary liked him at once. He was not like anybody she had met before.

"Where is your garden?" he asked.

Mary's face became red. She looked at him for a long time. "Can you keep a secret?" she said at last. "It's a very big secret. I have stolen a garden. Nobody wants it, nobody takes care of it, and they are going to let it die."

"Where is it?" asked Dickon softly.

She took him to the door under the ivy, and they went in. Dickon looked around with wide eyes. "It's like being in a dream," he said.

He went from tree to tree and cut some of the branches with his knife. "Look," he said. "This one is dry, but this one is green inside. It's alive! These roses are alive. We can make this garden beautiful again."

Mary was happier than she had ever been. They worked together all morning. Dickon was stronger and faster than Mary, and he knew the name of every plant. The robin watched them and sang.

"Does anybody know about this garden?" Dickon asked.

"No. You're the first. Will you tell anybody?"

"Never," said Dickon. "It's safe with me. We'll come here every day."

When Mary came home that afternoon, Martha had news. "Mr Craven is here," she said. "He wants to see you."

Mary was afraid. She went into his room. He was not ugly, but he had a tired, sad face and one shoulder was higher than the other.

"Do you need anything?" he asked.

"Could I have a bit of earth?" said Mary. "To plant seeds?"

He looked at her for a moment. "Take as much earth as you want," he said kindly.

chapters.title: Chapter 6. The Boy in the Bed
chapters.text:
That night Mary heard the crying again. This time she took a candle and followed the sound through dark corridors. At the end of one corridor there was a door with a light under it. She opened it.

In a big bed lay a thin, pale boy. He had large grey eyes and a lot of dark hair. He stopped crying and looked at her.

"Are you a ghost?" he whispered.

"No," said Mary. "I'm Mary Lennox. Mr Craven is my uncle. Who are you?"

"I'm Colin Craven. Mr Craven is my father."

Mary was very surprised. Nobody had told her that she had a cousin!

Colin told her about his life. He was always in bed. His back was weak, and everybody thought he was going to have a crooked back like his father. "Perhaps I'm going to die," he said. "Everyone thinks so. My father doesn't want to see me, because my mother died when I was born. He hates to look at me."

"Do you ever go outside?" asked Mary.

"No. People look at me, and I don't like it."

Then Mary told him about the moor, about Dickon and his animals, and about the robin. Colin listened with big eyes. Then she told him about a garden that was locked for ten years.

"I want to see that garden," said Colin. "I'm going to make them open it."

"No!" cried Mary. "If everybody knows, it won't be a secret. Please wait. Maybe one day we can go there together, secretly."

Colin thought about it. "All right," he said. "Come back tomorrow. You must come every day."

chapters.title: Chapter 7. A Terrible Night
chapters.text:
After that, Mary visited Colin every day. They talked and laughed together. Colin laughed more in one week than in all his life before. The servants were very surprised. Before, he was always angry and sad, and he shouted at everybody.

But one day it rained a lot, and Mary went to the garden with Dickon when the rain stopped. She did not visit Colin. When she came home, he was very angry.

"You're a selfish girl!" he shouted. "You went to that boy and forgot about me!"

"You're more selfish than me!" Mary shouted back. "You're the most selfish boy in the world!" And she left.

That night Mary woke up. Colin was screaming, and the whole house could hear him. The servants did not know what to do. Mary ran to his room, very angry.

"Stop it!" she shouted. "Stop it now! I hate you! Everybody hates you!"

Colin was so surprised that he stopped screaming. He was shaking and crying. "I felt a lump on my back," he said. "I'm going to have a crooked back, and then I'm going to die."

"Turn over," said Mary. "Let me see."

She looked carefully at his thin back. "There isn't any lump," she said. "It's only your bones, because you're so thin. My back has the same bones. You are not going to die."

Colin looked at her. For years people had whispered around him and said he was weak and ill. Nobody had ever said anything like this.

"Really?" he asked.

"Really," said Mary.

Colin lay down quietly. "Mary," he said, "will you tell me about the garden again?" She held his hand and talked softly about the spring until he fell asleep.

chapters.title: Chapter 8. Colin Sees the Garden
chapters.text:
The next day Dickon came to see Colin. He brought his little fox, a crow and two small lambs. Colin could not believe his eyes. He touched the animals and laughed and laughed.

"I'm going to see the garden," he said. "I'm going this week."

Colin told the gardeners to stay away from the garden paths. Nobody could disobey him, because he was the master's son. Then Dickon pushed him in his wheelchair, and Mary walked next to him. They went along the paths, through the door under the ivy, and into the secret garden.

Colin looked around. It was spring now, and the garden was full of colour. There were yellow and purple flowers everywhere. The trees had pink and white flowers, and the roses had new green leaves. Birds were singing.

"I'm going to get well!" Colin cried. "I'm going to live for ever and ever!"

They spent the whole afternoon there. Suddenly Mary saw a face on top of the wall. It was old Ben Weatherstaff, on a ladder.

"What are you doing in here?" he said angrily. Then he saw the boy in the wheelchair. "Are you the poor boy with the crooked back? And the weak legs?"

Colin's face became red. "I haven't got a crooked back!" he shouted. "My legs are not weak!"

He pushed off his blanket. Dickon held his arm. And slowly Colin stood up. He was standing on his own feet!

"Look at me!" he said to Ben.

The old man began to cry. "Nobody told me the truth," he said. "They said you were going to die."

"Well, I'm not," said Colin.

chapters.title: Chapter 9. Magic
chapters.text:
After that day, Colin went to the garden every morning. Ben Weatherstaff helped them, and he promised to keep the secret. Every day Colin walked a little more. At first he walked slowly and held onto a tree. After some weeks he could walk round the whole garden, and later he could even run.

"There is Magic in this garden," Colin said one day. "It makes the flowers grow, and it is making me strong. I'm going to be a scientist and study it."

Every morning the children sat under a tree and said, "The Magic is in me. The Magic is making me well."

But Colin did not want the doctor or the servants to know about his legs. "I want to show my father first," he said. "When he comes home, I'm going to walk to him. It will be a surprise."

So in the house Colin still sat in his wheelchair and pretended to be ill. It was not easy. He and Mary were always hungry now after the fresh air, and they ate a lot of food. The servants did not understand. "Master Colin is ill, but his face is getting fatter every day," they said. Sometimes the children laughed so much that they had to hide their faces in the pillows.

Dickon's mother knew the secret, because Dickon told her everything. One day she came to the garden with a basket of fresh bread and milk for them. She was a warm, wise woman. She looked at Colin and put her arms around him.

"Your mother would be very happy to see you now," she said. "Your father must come home. He must see you."

chapters.title: Chapter 10. Coming Home
chapters.text:
All this time Mr Craven was far away. He was travelling in Europe, in beautiful places, but he was always sad. For ten years he had thought only about his dead wife. He never thought about his son.

But one evening, beside a quiet lake in Austria, he suddenly felt calm. For the first time in years, his heart felt lighter. He did not know it, but at that time Colin was standing in the garden and shouting, "I'm going to live for ever!"

Some weeks later Mr Craven had a dream. He heard his wife's voice. "Archie," she said, "I am in the garden."

The next morning he got a letter from Dickon's mother. "Please come home, sir," she wrote. "I think you will be glad."

Mr Craven travelled home at once. He did not go to the house. He walked straight to the old garden. The door was still covered with ivy. But when he came near, he heard sounds inside. He heard children running and laughing.

Suddenly the door opened, and a tall, strong boy ran out, straight into his arms. He had grey eyes, just like his wife's eyes.

Mr Craven could not speak.

"Father," said the boy, "I'm Colin. You can't believe it. I can hardly believe it myself. It was the garden, and Mary, and Dickon, and the Magic. I'm well now. I'm going to live for ever and ever!"

Mr Craven put his hands on his son's shoulders. His eyes were full of tears. Then Colin took him into the garden, and the children told him the whole story.

That afternoon the servants looked out of the windows and saw something wonderful. The master was walking across the lawn to the house. And next to him, with his head up high, walked Colin, as strong and healthy as any boy in Yorkshire.
